messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malia, a 65‑year‑old cybersecurity analyst who now lives alone after her husband’s death, was still on her way home from a late shift when the world collapsed around her. A delivery truck, swerving to avoid a pothole, slammed into the rear of her car, sending the vehicle spinning and breaking apart. The impact lodged a twisted metal beam into her chest, and a spray of diesel fumes filled the cabin. The moment she came to, her heart was pounding, her vision blurred, and the smell of burning rubber clung to her senses. Even now, years later, she says that whenever she thinks about the frightening event she can sometimes smell the diesel and the burnt rubber that she smelt then—an olfactory recall that instantly pulls her back into that night. She remembers the shattered glass as a series of sharp, jagged images—visual memories that flash whenever she tries to move her hand, and the pain in her ribs and shoulders recurs as a vivid pain recall, as if the body still knows the exact pressure that slammed into it. The memory, in this way, keeps her trapped in the moment, constantly reminding her that her body can no longer be trusted, feeding the negative appraisal that “my body is unreliable” and the sense of injustice that “what happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it.” The very fact that these memories surface so vividly also keeps her awake, her mind racing at night when she wakes to check whether the hallway is still safe—night vigilance that follows the same pattern as her daytime fear of the unknown. Because of these negative appraisals, Malia has fallen into a cycle of maladaptive strategies. She says she goes over and over why the event happened to her, a rumination that she believes might somehow prevent it from happening again. The thought that her body is unreliable and that she has been wronged leads her to try to erase the memory of the event altogether, an attempt to protect herself from the pain and the guilt she feels. Her attempts to erase the memory force her to keep her mind busy with other thoughts, but this avoidance also keeps her from addressing the raw emotions that come with the memory. At the same time, the belief that she is unfairly exposed to others—“I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me”—drives her to stay constantly alert, to keep her fingers on the keys and her eyes on the security feed, so that she can detect any sign of danger. The need for vigilance keeps her from fully disengaging from the world, and the fear that she might slip again makes her feel trapped in a state of hyper‑alertness. Threat, once triggered by the memory’s return, pushes Malia further into her maladaptive patterns. The vivid images and the smell of diesel in the air make her feel as though the crash could recur, and she wakes during the night to check whether she is safe—waking alert that feeds the same vigilance that fuels her rumination. As she becomes more alert, she feels a compulsion to avoid any feelings that might arise, whether negative or positive, because she believes that any emotion could open the door for the past to intrude. The threat of being harmed again reinforces her negative appraisal of her body’s unreliability, and in turn, the appraisal heightens her threat vigilance. The threat also forces her to re‑experience the memory, because the body’s sense of danger triggers her to replay the visual memories and the pain recall until she feels the old fear settle once more. The loop tightens: threat leads to memory, memory to threat, and both fuel the negative appraisal that drives her avoidance. Malia’s maladaptive strategies have begun to shape the very memories she seeks to erase. Each attempt to wipe the memory from her mind brings it back in a new form: a sudden flash of the twisted metal, the hiss of diesel, the echo of the driver’s voice. She says that trying to forget is like trying to shut off a lamp by pulling the switch; the light flickers back on. The same way, her constant vigilance—her feeling that she has to be alert to keep herself safe—makes her even more likely to notice the same triggers in everyday life. In the workplace, when her screen flickers or a colleague’s voice rises too high, she’s startled, convinced the danger is imminent. The fear that her body may betray her again has seeped into her professional life; she now avoids open‑air meetings and prefers the quiet of her office, where she can keep all her systems under close watch. This avoidance has strained her relationship with her team, who view her as distant and uncooperative, and it has made her job—once a source of pride and intellectual challenge—a constant reminder that she cannot fully trust herself. Malia finally sought help after a week of not being able to turn off her laptop. The night before, she woke again and again, checking whether the hallway was still dark, and when she finally fell asleep she woke in a state of terror, shaking and breathing hard, the smell of diesel invading her thoughts. She realized that her hyper‑alertness had become a self‑fulfilling nightmare; the very vigilance she used to keep herself safe now made her feel perpetually unsafe. What frightened her most was that she could no longer differentiate between real danger and imagined threat, and she was terrified that she would one day lose her job, her sense of safety, and the small, fragile dignity she still clung to. In therapy she hopes to untangle the vicious circle of threat, memory, and appraisal, and to regain trust in her own body and in her ability to navigate the world without the constant specter of a crash that never truly ended.
